course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 3
unit.description: Follow the Seven Years' War, the road to independence, the Revolution, the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution, and the first political parties from 1754 to 1800.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The Articles of Confederation
lesson.summary: How the states and the first national government were organized after independence, why the Articles of Confederation proved too weak, and how Congress organized the Northwest Territory.
learningGoals: Describe how new state constitutions distributed power.
Explain the structure and limits of the Articles of Confederation and why they led to calls for a stronger government.
Explain the significance of the Northwest Ordinance.
lesson.bigIdea: After independence, Americans feared concentrated power, so they created weak executives and a weak national government, and they then found that this arrangement could not meet the new nation's problems.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how different forms of government developed and changed as a result of the Revolutionary period. Compare what the new governments did with what their designers feared.

sections.title: New state constitutions

blocks.text: Many new state constitutions placed power in the hands of the legislative branch and maintained property qualifications for voting and citizenship. Americans had just fought against a distant executive power, so most states gave their governors limited powers and made legislatures the strongest branch. Many constitutions included declarations of rights that protected individual liberties.
Massachusetts's 1780 constitution was written by a convention elected for that purpose and approved by voters, which became a model for later constitution making.

sections.takeaway: State constitutions gave the most power to legislatures, limited governors, and protected rights.

sections.title: The Articles of Confederation

blocks.text: The Articles of Confederation unified the newly independent states, creating a central government with limited power. Congress was the only branch of the national government. Each state had one vote, there was no president, and the national government had no power to tax or to regulate trade among the states. Important laws required the approval of nine of the thirteen states, and changing the Articles required the agreement of all thirteen. The Articles were adopted by Congress in 1777 and went into force in 1781 after all the states had ratified them.

The new government won the war and negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783. After the Revolution, however, difficulties over international trade, finances, interstate commerce, foreign relations, and internal unrest led to calls for a stronger central government. Congress had to ask the states for money and could not make them pay. States set up trade barriers against one another, Britain refused to leave forts in the Northwest, and Spain closed the Mississippi River to American navigation in 1784, hurting western settlers.

In 1786–1787, Shays' Rebellion, in which indebted farmers in western Massachusetts shut down courts to stop foreclosures, frightened many leaders. The national government had no army to put down the rebellion and the state had to raise a militia on its own. To many Americans, the episode showed the need for a government able to keep order.

sections.takeaway: The Articles preserved state power and won the war, but a government without the power to tax or regulate trade could not solve postwar problems.

sections.title: Settling the West

blocks.text: As settlers moved westward during the 1780s, Congress enacted the Northwest Ordinance for admitting new states. The Land Ordinance of 1785 set up a system for surveying and selling western land in orderly townships and set aside land for public schools. The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 provided for governing the territory north of the Ohio River and a path to statehood on equal terms with the original states once a territory reached a certain population. The ordinance promoted public education, the protection of private property, and a ban on slavery in the Northwest Territory.

These laws were among the most lasting achievements of the Confederation Congress, and they created a model for how the nation would expand. They did not recognize the land claims of the Native peoples who lived in the region, which led to conflict.

sections.takeaway: The Northwest Ordinance created a lasting model for admitting new states and banned slavery in the Northwest Territory.

connections.title: Revising the Articles
connections.body: The weaknesses of the Articles led to a convention in Philadelphia. Topic 3.8 follows that meeting and the debate over ratification.
connections.transferQuestion: Which problem under the Articles do you think most convinced leaders that a stronger government was needed?
connections.feedback: A strong answer picks a specific problem, such as the lack of a power to tax or Shays' Rebellion, and explains how a stronger government would address it.
